summary: A status report that gathers in one place information about networked information retrieval tools of the time, their developers, interested organizations, and related activities. It is a survey meant to raise awareness, not a protocol specification.

eli5.summary: A guide listing the tools people used to find stuff online, who made them, and who was working on them.

subtitle: A 1994 snapshot of the tools, people and groups behind finding information on the early Internet.

tldr.problem: By 1994 many tools had appeared for finding and fetching information across the Internet, and the people building and using them had no single place to learn what existed or who was behind it.
tldr.mechanism: The Networked Information Retrieval Working Group collected filled-in templates from tool and group contacts and compiled them into one report covering archie, Gopher, WAIS, the World Wide Web, WHOIS, X.500 and more.
tldr.outcome: The result is a long catalogue of tools and groups as they stood in 1993 and 1994. It specifies no protocol, and it was meant to be a living document updated yearly.

facts.label: Gopher servers (Dec 1993)
facts.value: About 4800, about a third with Gopher+

today: RFC 1689 is an Informational RFC from August 1994 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a snapshot of the tools and groups of that time, and its figures are dated to late 1993 and early 1994, not to the present.

sections.title: Why a Status Report
sections.content:
RFC 1689 is an Informational memo edited by J. Foster, also published as RARE Technical Report 13 and FYI 25. It says plainly that it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind. Its purpose is to increase awareness of Networked Information Retrieval (NIR) by bringing into one place the NIR tools, their developers, interested organisations and other activities around producing, spreading and supporting those tools.

The report opens by noting that in the previous two and a half years there had been widespread adoption of archie servers, Wide Area Information Servers (WAIS), the Internet gopher and the World Wide Web (WWW). It also observes that networked information retrieval was in its infancy compared with traditional retrieval systems: thesaurus construction, boolean searching and classification control were under discussion but not yet in widespread use.

The editors intended it to be a living document held on-line, with each section updatable separately and the full document refreshed once a year as a snapshot.
sections.eli5: Lots of new ways to look things up on the Internet appeared at once. This report puts them all in one place so people can see what exists and who to ask.

sections.title: How the Information Was Collected
sections.content:
The content was gathered over the network from the contact for each tool or group, using two templates: the NIR Tool Template (Appendix A) and the NIR Group Template (Appendix B). The tool template asks how and where to get the software, the documentation, demonstration sites and so on. The group template asks for the aim and purpose of the group, its current tasks, mailing lists and document archives.

The templates were discussed by the NIR working group in Boston (July 1992) and then on the mailing list. The initial draft was discussed in Washington (November 1992) and revised at later meetings. Before the RFC was submitted, independent reviewers from around the world each checked a few templates for accuracy and currency.

Updates go to the address nir-updates@cnidr.org, because CNIDR agreed to host the report and accept updates from template maintainers. The report and templates could also be fetched from the UK Mailbase server by anonymous ftp, gopher, WWW or email.
sections.eli5: The authors sent every tool maker the same questionnaire and pasted the answers together, then asked other people to check the answers were right.

sections.title: Kinds of NIR Tool
sections.content:
Section 5 offers a simple classification, which the RFC stresses is only one possible ordering. Techniques reappear, so seemingly different tools often do similar jobs.

  • Interactive information delivery (Gopher, World Wide Web): ways to browse information across the network without logging in or knowing where to look first. Both share a maintenance problem, because there is no automated way to update links when documents move or disappear.
  • Directory services (WHOIS, X.500): lookup of people (white pages) or of services and providers (yellow pages). The RFC notes that despite years of effort there was still no single white pages directory for the entire Internet, and yellow pages were even less developed.
  • Indexing services (archie, Veronica, online library catalogs): searchable catalogs of information, starting with access to library card catalogs and moving to indexing network-based information.
  • Text-based indexing (WAIS): indexes the text of the target documents themselves as well as descriptions of what a server holds.
sections.eli5: There are tools for wandering around (browsing), tools for looking up people, and tools that build giant card catalogs so you can search instead of wander.

sections.title: Gopher: Menus and Selector Strings
sections.content:
The tool entry for the Internet Gopher describes a client/distributed-server document search and retrieval protocol originally developed at the University of Minnesota. The RFC calls it "fiercely simple": it is connectionless (stateless) and uses TCP reliable streams. A client connects to a server over TCP and sends a one-line text selector string. The server returns the matching item (a file, a directory listing or a link to another service) and immediately closes the connection.

Directory listings come back as lines ending in carriage-return line-feed. Each line starts with a one-character item type tag, then a display string, then tab-delimited fields giving the selector string, the host domain name and the port number. Users see what looks like a hierarchy of directories, but the links form a graph rather than a simple rooted tree, and links can lead to services such as cso servers, telnet sessions, other gopher servers and gateway servers.

The protocol itself is described in RFC 1436. Extensions known together as Gopher+ add meta-information, alternate views of documents (text, postscript, rtf and so on) and electronic forms, and are upward compatible with the original protocol. As of December 1993, about a third of the roughly 4800 gopher servers supported Gopher+.
sections.eli5: Gopher is like a friendly librarian. You walk up, say one line, get exactly one thing handed to you, and then the librarian is ready for the next person.

sections.title: Search Services: archie, Veronica and WAIS
sections.content:
archie began as a project to catalog the contents of hundreds of ftp-accessible file archives. It gathers location, name and other details into an index database that users search through telnet, stand-alone clients (which use the Prospero protocol), gopher, WWW or electronic mail. The report gives figures as of November 1993: over 2,100,000 filenames on over 1,200 sites, served by about 30 geographically distributed archie servers.

Veronica set out to do for Gopher what archie did for ftp. A central server periodically scans the menu hierarchies of the listed gopher servers and builds a title index that any gopher client can search. The Veronica entry reports indexes to more than 3200 gopher servers as of February 1994, with an estimated 1,200,000 queries served in that month.

WAIS (Wide Area Information Servers) differs because it indexes the text of documents, not just descriptions. Early clients take natural-language queries, drop common words, rank matching documents with a simple statistical weighting, and let the user feed results back to refine later searches (relevance feedback). The WAIS entry says it uses a single computer-to-computer protocol, NISO Z39.50-1988. Both commercial versions and the free freeWAIS from CNIDR existed.
sections.eli5: archie and Veronica are card catalogs for file collections and for Gopher menus. WAIS is a catalog that reads inside the books, and it gets better when you tell it which results you liked.

sections.title: The World Wide Web in 1994
sections.content:
The WWW entry describes a project that merges networked information with hypertext into a global information system. W3 uses a seamless information space, the "web", in which all objects, including those reached through earlier protocols such as wais, gopher and ftp, exist. It was originally aimed at the High Energy Physics community, and the entry calls it the most advanced information system deployed on the Internet at that time.

For readers, the web consists of documents and links. Indexes are special documents that are searched rather than read, and the result of a search is another "virtual" document containing links. A simple protocol, HTTP, lets a browser ask a remote information server for a keyword search. Following a link and giving keywords are described as the only operations needed.

For information providers, running the W3 server and pointing it at an existing directory structure is enough, because the server generates the hypertext view automatically. Gateways exist to systems such as Oracle, WAIS and Digital's VMS/Help. The model also allows a smart browser and a smart server to negotiate the data format. The entry points newcomers to the NCSA Mosaic browser, the Cello browser for Windows and the Lynx full-screen interface.
sections.eli5: On the web every page is a room, and the links are doors to other rooms. You only need to know how to click a door or type what you are looking for.

sections.title: Directory and Lookup Tools
sections.content:
Several entries deal with finding people and services. WHOIS was one of the first directory services on the Internet, a simple white pages service created to track key network contacts for the early DARPA-sponsored Internet. Its entry says the service was defined in 1985 and has since become a distributed service, with the InterNIC Registration Services hosting a WHOIS registry of domains, networks and related contacts. Work was underway on WHOIS++, which is backwards-compatible and adds a richer query syntax plus an index service built on "forward knowledge" that routes a query to base-level servers likely to hold the answer.

X.500 is an international standard for a distributed global directory, used mainly for white pages. Its first solid version was released in 1988, and its entry notes LDAP-based clients and a gopher gateway to X.500. Netfind is not a directory in the usual sense: given a person's name and a rough description of their workplace, it uses several Internet services and heuristics to find information about them, covering over 5 million people in over 9,000 domains when last measured.

Other entries round out the picture. Prospero organizes references to files scattered across the Internet as if they were on a local system, Alex exposes anonymous ftp sites as a filesystem through a user-level NFS server, and HYTELNET is a hypertext guide to telnet-accessible sites such as library catalogs.
sections.eli5: Some tools are phone books for people on the Internet. Others are helpers that make far-away files look like they are on your own computer.

sections.title: The Groups Behind NIR
sections.content:
Section 7 describes the organisations and working groups active in the field, grouped by sponsor. They include the Coalition for Networked Information (CNI) with its subgroups, the Clearinghouse for Networked Information Discovery and Retrieval (CNIDR), several IETF groups (including Uniform Resource Identifiers and the joint IETF/RARE NIR working group itself), the IRTF Research Group on Resource Discovery and Directory Service, the NISO Z39.50 Implementors Group, the RARE Information Services and User Support Working Group, and the USMARC and OCLC cataloging efforts.

CNI is described as founded in March 1990 and as a partnership of the Association of Research Libraries, CAUSE and EDUCOM. Its task force involved more than 190 institutions and organizations.

The appendices add an email list and newsgroup directory (Appendix C) and a "Coming Attractions" list (Appendix D) of tools not yet in widespread use: Hyper-G, Soft Pages and WHOIS++. Appendix E, for tools that have fallen out of use, was empty. Appendix F, a record of closed groups, listed IAFA and the Z39.50 Interoperability Testbed.
sections.eli5: Behind every tool there are teams and clubs working on it. The report lists the clubs, what each one is trying to do and how to join their mailing lists.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. Individual tool entries mention security in passing. For example, the Prospero entry lists four ways of authenticating clients: a simple client assertion of identity, a trusted port mechanism similar to the Berkeley UNIX R commands, a simple cleartext password mechanism, and Kerberos version 5. The X.500 entry says that protocol has a number of security features, implemented differently in the various servers.
sections.eli5: The report does not talk about keeping things safe, apart from a few notes inside the descriptions of individual tools.
